title: 1 Samuel 28:15–25
context: The figure WEB calls Samuel repeats the LORD’s judgment: the kingdom is given to David, and Saul and his sons will die the next day. Saul collapses, and the woman and his servants persuade him to eat before he leaves in the night. How the appearance is understood remains an interpretive question across traditions.

verses.text: Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up?” Saul answered, “I am very distressed; for the Philistines make war against me, and God has departed from me, and answers me no more, by prophets, or by dreams. Therefore I have called you, that you may make known to me what I shall do.”
verses.arminianNotes: WEB reads: Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me, to bring me up?” Saul explains, “God has departed from me.” Arminian readers see Saul’s own confession of the separation his disobedience brought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Saul acknowledging God’s silence. Interpreters who see a genuine appearance take the speaker as Samuel; others read the narrator as describing the figure as it appeared, and the text does not settle the matter for every reader.

verses.text: Samuel said, “Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has departed from you and has become your adversary?
verses.arminianNotes: The figure asks, “Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has departed from you and has become your adversary?” Arminian readers see the message confirming that Saul cannot bypass God through other means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment reaffirmed. Readers in both traditions commonly note that the message is consistent with Samuel’s earlier prophecies, a point often raised by those who hold the appearance was genuine.

verses.text: The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me. The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, even to David.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, even to David.” Arminian readers see the word of 1 Samuel 15:28 repeated, now naming David directly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s earlier verdict restated with David named. The message centers on the LORD’s action and word, and whatever reading of the appearance one holds, its content agrees with earlier prophecy.

verses.text: Because you didn’t obey the LORD’s voice, and didn’t execute his fierce wrath on Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you today.
verses.arminianNotes: “Because you didn’t obey the LORD’s voice, and didn’t execute his fierce wrath on Amalek.” Arminian readers see judgment tied explicitly to Saul’s disobedience recorded in chapter 15.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reason for judgment stated clearly. The verse reminds readers that Saul’s loss of the kingdom rests on concrete disobedience to God’s command, which both traditions affirm.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD will deliver Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines; and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will deliver the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes: The figure says, “tomorrow you and your sons will be with me,” and Israel will fall to the Philistines. Arminian readers see a sobering announcement of death that Saul can no longer escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment pronounced as certain. Interpreters differ on what “with me” implies about the state of the dead, and the verse is better read as announcing death than as describing the afterlife in detail.

verses.text: Then Saul fell immediately his full length on the earth, and was terrified, because of Samuel’s words. There was no strength in him, for he had eaten no bread all day long or all night long.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul falls full length, terrified “because of Samuel’s words,” weak from not eating. Arminian readers see the crushing effect of hearing judgment with no further hope offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a king undone by the message. The note that Saul had not eaten adds physical weakness to spiritual despair, preparing for the meal scene that follows.

verses.text: The woman came to Saul and saw that he was very troubled, and said to him, “Behold, your servant has listened to your voice, and I have put my life in my hand, and have listened to your words which you spoke to me.
verses.arminianNotes: The woman says, “I have put my life in my hand, and have listened to your words.” Arminian readers see her reminding Saul of the risk she took and appealing to him in return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see her concern for the shaken king. The narrator portrays her with surprising sympathy here, without approving the practice the chapter has already shown to be forbidden.

verses.text: Now therefore, please listen also to the voice of your servant, and let me set a morsel of bread before you. Eat, that you may have strength when you go on your way.”
verses.arminianNotes: She urges, “let me set a morsel of bread before you. Eat, that you may have strength.” Arminian readers see simple kindness offered to a desperate man on the eve of battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see ordinary compassion in her offer. The contrast is striking: Saul receives practical care from a medium while hearing no answer from the God he has forsaken.

verses.text: But he refused, and said, “I will not eat.” But his servants, together with the woman, constrained him; and he listened to their voice. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says, “I will not eat,” but his servants and the woman persuade him, and he sits on the bed. Arminian readers see a king so shaken that he must be urged to take care of himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Saul’s collapse of strength and will. The scene highlights human frailty and the mercy of small comforts even in the shadow of judgment.

verses.text: The woman had a fattened calf in the house. She hurried and killed it; and she took flour and kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread of it.
verses.arminianNotes: The woman quickly kills a fattened calf and bakes unleavened bread. Arminian readers see generous hospitality that contrasts with the bleak message Saul has just received.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a lavish meal prepared in haste. The detail adds a somber tone, since the meal comes on the night before Saul’s death in battle.

verses.text: She brought it before Saul and before his servants, and they ate. Then they rose up and went away that night.
verses.arminianNotes: She serves Saul and his servants, and “they rose up and went away that night.” Arminian readers see the final night of Saul’s life ending in darkness and departure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrative close quietly, leaving Saul to face the battle announced in verse 19. The chapter ends without resolving every question raised by the encounter at Endor.
